extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and metaphysical/philosophical readers (creative writers interested in imagination and the theory of poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and guidance on the nature, genesis, and creative function of the Imagination (versus Fancy), together with principles for philosophical style, terminology, and how to address readers and critics; aimed at informing poetic production and genial criticism in the fine arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justified use of technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use technical terms in philosophy whenever they tend to preclude confusion of thought, and when they assist the memory by the exclusive singleness of their meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives examples (multeity for kind-without-degree; potence and the coinage potenziate) and states the privilege is legitimate where no adequate existing term exists, to express kind-abstractions, to preserve correspondence in sound, or to avoid repeated circumlocution. Do not invent terms where a positive law (an adequate term) already exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity over novelty of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual and new-coined words are doubtless an evil; but vagueness, confusion, and imperfect conveyance of our thoughts, are a far greater [evil].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference should be given to terms that make thought clear and intelligible; novelty of wording is defensible only if it reduces confusion and increases precision. Beware coining words that merely produce learned jargon without clearer conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must reconcile reason with common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the two-fold function of philosophy to reconcile reason with common sense, and to elevate common sense into reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical systems should not dismiss the faith of common humanity; rather, they should show how ordinary realistic intuitions fit into reasoned theory. Philosophic argument must render common sense intelligible within a systematic framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: True metaphysics: clear, solid, pertinent reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reasoning be clear, solid and pertinent, the truth deduced can never be the less valuable on account of the depth from which it may have been drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of metaphysics (and by extension writers of imaginative theory) must prioritize argumentative rigor and pertinence — clarity and logical force vindicate conclusions even if they are deep or unfamiliar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Imagination from Fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination (or shaping and modifying power) is distinct from the fancy (the aggregative and associative power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate faculties: aggregation/association (fancy) is not identical with the active, constructive, shaping operation of Imagination. In practice, both may co-occur, but the work effected by each is distinct and different — assign functions explicitly when analyzing or producing poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active, constructive conception of knowing/creative intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is correlative to being. Knowledge without a correspondent reality is no knowledge; to know is in its very essence a verb active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach poetic and philosophical creation as active processes: knowledge and imagination produce forms rather than merely passively reflect them. Creative work should embody doing/constructing rather than only representing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek an absolute immediate ground for intelligibility (self-consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some absolute truth capable of communicating to other positions a certainty which it has not itself borrowed; a truth self-grounded, unconditional and known by its own light — expressed as the SUM or I AM (spirit, self, self-consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In building a systematic theory (of mind, imagination, or art), anchor arguments in an immediate principle that provides unity and prevents infinite regress. For Coleridge this is self-consciousness; in creative theory, identify and make explicit the foundational intuition or principle that grounds your claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art/Imagination arises from the interpenetration of opposing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a power with two contrary forces (one tending to expand infinitely, the other to apprehend or find itself); the counteraction of two such indestructible, infinite forces will produce a tertium aliquid — a finite generation by interpenetration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model imaginative creation as the productive tension of opposites (e.g., centrifugal/centripetal). In practice, create works that embody dynamic tension rather than mere neutralization; the 'third' produced by conflict is the creative object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination is an act of will and requires freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The self-conscious spirit must in some sense dissolve identity to be conscious of it, which implies an act; intelligence or self-consciousness is impossible, except by and in a will. The self-conscious spirit therefore is a will; and freedom must be assumed as a ground of philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative practice presupposes volition and freedom; poets and critics should treat imaginative production as willed activity rather than deterministic concatenation. Theorizing about art should acknowledge agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imethodical eclecticism; preserve system and logical connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Imethodical aphorisming eclectics dismiss system and logical connection, pick and choose whatever is plausible and showy, and thereby engender a popular counterfeit of true philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing criticism or theoretical prose, prioritize systematic coherence and logical links over standalone glittering sentences or fashionable fragments. Resist assembling apparent insights without demonstrating their interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical analogy cautiously to clarify philosophical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: An imitation of the mathematical method (e.g., negative quantities, opposites) can yield useful hints for establishing and pacifying the unsettled domain of philosophy; apply such positions mutatis mutandis to philosophical subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow formal structures (like opposing quantities, neutrality vs tertium) to illuminate creative principles, but translate analogies carefully — they are heuristic aids, not literal reductions of poetic process to algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor dense theoretical material to audience and context
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend advises withdrawing the dense Chapter on the Imagination from a volume intended as an introduction to poems and reserving it for an announced treatise; dense metaphysical chapters may bewilder the majority of poetry readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or presenting theory alongside creative work, consider audience expectations and placement: reserve heavy philosophical exposition for treatises and keep poetry collections accessible, or provide signposting and contextual framing so readers can follow.
